rows.en_context: Nevertheless we shall take care not to confuse a path of type $I$ with the opposite path of type $I^{\opp}$, the source of the one being the target of the other and conversely. This is to say that a path must be seen as \textit{more} than a mere functor \[ I \longrightarrow X, \] we must in addition give ourselves the \textit{orientation of $I$} as forming part of the path structure. So the reasonable formal definition, which fits the intuition of a path as going from a well-defined \textit{source} toward an equally well-defined \textit{target}, is that a path (defined in terms of an interval category $I$) is the datum of a pair $(\omega,c)$, where $\omega$ is an orientation of $I$, and $c$ a functor $c : I \longrightarrow X$. When we look at the category of paths of a fixed ``type'', this \textit{type} is $(I,\omega)$, and not $I$. It is when $\omega$ is fixed once and for all that this category can with impunity be identified with $\uHom(I,X)$ without more.
